rv.q: This exuberantly silly musical adaptation of the Nickelodeon cartoon series is a candy-colored rush of joy that somehow manages to be both faithfully nonsensical and surprisingly touching.

This rollicking musical adaptation of the beloved Nickelodeon cartoon series is a fizzy, exuberant show that captures all the innocent joy and silly humor of the source material while adding sophisticated theatrical craftsmanship.
Check your preconceptions at the door and enjoy the ride.
The show is a sugar rush of color, music, and movement that somehow manages to be both completely faithful to the source material and surprisingly sophisticated in its theatrical ambitions.

Now the grand playhouse has been transformed into a brightly festive Bikini Bottom, underwater home of that bubbly, lovable cartoon character and cultural phenomenon SpongeBob SquarePants, making his Broadway debut in a self-titled musical that’s an absolute delight.
The SpongeBob musical is a triumph of theatrical imagination that transforms Nickelodeon's cartoon into something genuinely moving and spectacular.

The musical is sufficiently skillfully assembled that family audiences seeking an antidote to too much reality will likely take the deep dive to Bikini Bottom looking for that “Best Day Ever,” as one of the songs goes.
This is not a piece that will create many new believers.

For what it's worth - and we're talking millions of dollars here - you are never going to see as convincing an impersonation of a two-dimensional cartoon by a three-dimensional human as that provided by Ethan Slater at the Palace Theater. Mr.

I can’t see recommending this show to anyone except true “SpongeBob” buffs.
This musical is one of the best musicals on Broadway right now, and is certainly the best musical of the season.
For all that the multi-colored SpongeBob musical cavalcade is a party for the eyes and ears, it is also political—radical even.
Just a simple Sponge? "SpongeBob," at the Palace Theatre, is simply a pleasure.
SpongeBob SquarePants The Broadway Musical, has captured all the silly, goofy, broadly camp, good-natured fun of the Nickelodeon TV series.
Theatrical staging is a continuous giddy delight.
That aside, if you're up for a little anarchic fun, dive right in.
Holiday cheer has arrived — in the form of 'nautical nonsense.'
Overall, it's an entertaining, if overstuffed and a bit too experimental, homage to the long-running cartoon.
Otherwise, it’s a tame evening for those who enter the Palace gates without a preexisting affinity for SpongeBob SquarePants.
It’s all admirably imaginative.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this colorful adaptation, praising Ethan Slater's energetic performance and David Zinn's dazzling design, though some find it overstuffed. The show surprises skeptics with theatrical inventiveness and infectious optimism.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.
